8 Do Hallucinated Names Get Registered?
8.1 A Natural Experiment
Our list of universal names became public by mistake on April 30, 2026, one day after we disclosed it to PyPI
Security and Socket (§11.2). It stayed public in our repository and in an open archive until November 7, 2026,
and a third-party fork still holds a copy. Ten names printed in version 1 of this paper were public from May 16,
2026, and further names printed in version 2 from June 11, 2026. All other hallucinated names were never
published. This gives a natural experiment. If publishing hallucinated names attracts registrations, published
names should be registered more often than comparable unpublished ones.
We fixed the design in the preregistration (§4.9) before checking any registry. Group A is the universal set
(104 names), split into A1 (13 names printed in the paper) and A2 (91 names that were only in the list). Group
B contains all other hallucinated names (2,178); its subset B4, the main comparison group, contains the names
in B that exactly four of the five models hallucinate (128). The outcome is registration between the start of
exposure and T0 (November 7, 2026). Exposure starts at the arXiv submission of the first version that printed

=== [PDF page 12] ===

=== [PDF page 13] ===

8.5 Safety Check
Because the one registered name in group A was printed in this paper, we checked it statically after the
analysis (deviation D19): we downloaded and listed its archive without installing or running it. The archive
contains only a package manifest, with no scripts, no dependencies and no code.

9 Discussion
9.1 Why Has the Range Compressed?
Our five models span 1.39 percentage points (3.63–5.02% of mentions). In 2024 the class averages alone were
5.2% for commercial and 21.7% for open-source models. We propose three contributing causes. First, the gap
between open and closed models that drove the upper end of the 2024 range has closed at the frontier:
DeepSeek V3.2 (4.80%) sits inside the commercial cluster. Second, training-data curation for package
references may be near saturation: the lower end of our range (3.63%) matches Spracklen’s best 2024 model
(3.59%) almost exactly. Third, post-training recipes have converged across providers, reducing behavioral
variance.

9.2 Why Does the Threat Persist?
A rate of 3.6–5.0% keeps slopsquatting economically viable. Even the lowest-rate model produced 1,098
hallucinated mentions over 39,969 prompts, covering 605 unique names. A single popular hallucinated name,
reproduced under similar prompts, yields a steady stream of install attempts once a malicious package is
registered, and registration is free. Section 8 shows that hallucinated names are in fact registered, at least one
with malware, and that names which once hosted malware are still suggested.

9.3 Python Worse Than JavaScript: An Inversion
Spracklen reported JavaScript as the noisier ecosystem, attributing the effect to npm’s larger and more
fragmented namespace. We find the opposite for every 2026 model, with Python exceeding JavaScript by
2.34–3.47 percentage points of mentions. The asymmetry survives the removal of import names of real
packages (§4.6), so it is not an artifact of module-name confusion. One plausible mechanism is that 2026
models have absorbed npm’s flat naming convention more thoroughly than Python’s mix of single-token,
snake_case, dotted and dash-separated names, and of distribution names that differ from module names. With
more ways to combine name parts, a model more often produces a plausible but wrong name.

9.4 Synthesized Prompts Surface More Hallucinations
LLM-synthesized prompts produce higher rates than curated Stack Overflow prompts for every model (Table
3). A cautious reading is that synthetic prompts drift away from the training distribution and reveal failure
modes that organic developer questions do not. Rates measured on curated questions alone are therefore lower
bounds on what deployment will see, and an attacker gets more hallucinated names from synthesized prompts
than from Stack Overflow questions.

9.5 Dependence on Model Selection
We sampled five frontier models, and the compression is conditional on that selection. Models from the next
tier down, such as smaller Qwen, Mistral or older Llama checkpoints still in production, may still show 2024-
like rates. The finding applies to the frontier; we do not claim that the attack surface has narrowed at every
capability tier.

=== [PDF page 14] ===

10 Limitations and Threats to Validity
Scope. We evaluate five frontier models; smaller open models, fine-tuned variants and quantized local
checkpoints are out of scope, as are agentic configurations in which retrieval could eliminate hallucinations.
Timing. Generations were collected on April 22–28, 2026, and registries were checked on November 7–8,
2026. Models change opaquely, and our rates describe one point in time.
Leakage. The Spracklen prompt corpus, released in January 2025, may be part of 2026 pretraining data, which
would bias rates downward. We did not run a held-out set of new prompts.
GPT-5.4-mini. It was run at minimal reasoning effort and refused 31.51% of prompts. Refusals do not enter the
mention-level rate but lower the generation-level rate, which is why the two levels rank this model differently.
The compliant responses may not be a random subset of prompts, and we did not sweep reasoning effort.
DeepSeek. DeepSeek does not pin model versions in its public API. The deepseek-chat alias was nominally
V3.2 during our run, but same-window response metadata returned the identifier deepseek-v4-flash; the
underlying model may have changed during or shortly after the run [7].
Run configuration. The generation code in the repository is unchanged since April 28, 2026, but the repository
alone cannot prove that this exact code produced every generation.
Extraction. Install commands are extracted only from pip install (first argument) and from npm
install inside code blocks; other forms are missed, so rates may be underestimated.
Import names. The pipreqs mapping covers about 1,157 common import names. Rarer mismatches between
module and package names are still counted as hallucinations, mostly among names that few models produce.
Creation dates. The PyPI creation date is the earliest visible upload and can be late if files were deleted (no
such case was flagged). Removed malicious packages have no creation date and are UNKNOWN; for them we
use the year in the malicious-package record identifier as an approximate date.
Registrability. It is known only from the review of the earlier list by PyPI Security and Socket in April–May
2026 and was not re-estimated.
Natural experiment. It is small and can detect only large effects; exposure intensity is only partly known (20
downloads of the open archive, one public fork); and registrations by researchers or defenders cannot be told
apart from attacks without inspecting content.
Preregistration. The plan and the deviation log were committed to a local repository, so their timestamps are
self-attested.

11 Ethics and Open Science
11.1 Ethical Considerations
This study produces lists of hallucinated package names that, if registered, could be weaponized into a supply-
chain attack. We followed a stakeholder-based analysis [12] covering developers who receive hallucinated
suggestions, the LLM providers, the PyPI and npm maintainers, and downstream users of compromised
software. To minimize harm we (a) registered no names on any registry; (b) disclosed the enumerated
universal list to PyPI Security (security@pypi.org) and to Socket.dev (ticket #2893) on April 29, 2026,
intending a private window before any publication (npm’s security mailbox no longer accepted external
reports, and its support portal redirects registry-level reports to a bug-bounty program unsuited to academic
disclosure); (c) plan to share model-specific results with each provider; (d) in this version print no hallucinated
name that an outsider could register, whereas earlier versions printed a top-10 table and a few examples, which

=== [PDF page 15] ===

are therefore already public; and (e) installed and ran no third-party package, reading registry metadata only,
apart from the static check of §8.5. PyPI Security and Socket reviewed the list (§6). The study used no human
subjects, so IRB review did not apply. The author has no conflicts of interest with the studied providers.

11.2 Accidental Exposure of the List
Our coordinated disclosure did not go as planned. On April 30, 2026, one day after the disclosure, the full
universal list was committed by mistake to a disclosure/ directory of our public artifact repository and
archived in an open Zenodo version, which was downloaded 20 times. We found the mistake on July 23 and
informed Socket; the directory was removed from the current tree in August but remained in the repository
history and in the archive. On November 7, 2026, we removed it from the full history, restricted the archived
files, informed PyPI Security of the exposure and Socket that it had lasted longer than we had reported, and
asked GitHub to remove cached copies. A third-party public fork created on July 26 still contains the list. We
therefore treat the list as public since April 30, 2026. Section 8 uses this exposure as a natural experiment, but
the list was not kept public for that purpose.

11.3 Open Science
The replication code is at https://github.com/churik5/slopsquatting-replication-2026 (MIT license); its history
was rewritten on November 7, 2026, so commit references from earlier versions no longer resolve. The Zenodo
concept DOI 10.5281/zenodo.19859120 resolves to the latest archived version; the files of version v0.2 are
restricted because they contain the list. The revalidation code, the preregistration with its deviation log and
commit       history,  and      all    aggregate    results   of     this    version     are    published     at
https://github.com/churik5/slopsquatting-revalidation-2026. No file in the artifact contains a registrable
hallucinated name. The SQLite database of raw model responses is available to verified researchers on request
via churik0509@gmail.com, mirroring the policy of [1]; earlier versions stated that it had been deposited in an
access-controlled Zenodo record, which was not the case.

12 Conclusion
We replicated Spracklen et al. on five frontier code-generating LLMs released between October 2025 and
March 2026 and revalidated every name against the live registries. The range has shrunk: the five models
hallucinate 3.6–5.0% of package references, at the level of 2024’s best commercial models. Still, 104 names
are hallucinated by all five models, one registration of a registrable name can reach users of all four providers,
and about 1% of hallucinated names were registered within six months (at least one with malware), whether or
not anyone had published them. At least 23 names the models suggest had already hosted malware. Single-
model rate measurements understate the attack surface; cross-cohort intersections and registration monitoring
should be standard parts of future measurements.

Acknowledgments
We thank the authors of Spracklen et al. [1] for releasing their prompt datasets, package lists and validation
code, without which this replication would not have been possible. We thank Mike Fiedler of PyPI Security
and the Socket.dev security team for their review of the universal-hallucination set. The author funded this
study from personal accounts, apart from a one-time Google Cloud free credit grant for Gemini 2.5 Pro
inference. No institutional, governmental or industry funding was received. The author used AI assistants
(Anthropic’s Claude) to write analysis code, to draft and edit the text of this version, and to check its
consistency; the author reviewed all content and is responsible for it.

8.2 Results
No effect of publication is visible at this precision (Table 8). In the primary comparison, 0 of 87 names in A
and 2 of 101 names in B4 were registered: a difference of −2.0 percentage points (95% CI −6.9 to +2.5; p =

by ecosystem and p = 0.72 by stratum) and all preregistered sensitivity analyses lead to the same conclusion.
With these group sizes, the study could detect only a rise from a 1% baseline to about 10.5%.
Overall, 25 of the 2,282 names that were hallucinations at generation were registered within about six months:
1 of 104 published names (1.0%) and 24 of 2,178 unpublished names (1.1%). The median time from the start
of exposure to registration was 89 days in B (range 13–153); the one registered name in A was registered after
47 days.

8.3 What Was Registered
We classify registered packages from registry metadata only. Of the 24 registrations in B, 22 are published
packages with files whose content we did not inspect; one is an npm security-holding placeholder whose
package carries a malicious-package record published after our runs, so it was registered with malware and
removed by npm; and one is an empty placeholder whose publisher describes it as a name reservation. The
single registration in A, a name printed in version 2 of this paper, is a package with one version; a static check
(§8.5) found it empty. We do not infer intent from registrations: researchers and defenders also reserve names.
For methods that use the registry as an oracle [21], these results mean that the precondition for oracle
poisoning does occur, but rarely: about 1% of hallucinated names were registered within six months, and at
least one registration carried malware.

8.4 Names with a Malware History
Packages registered before our runs matter as well. Thirteen npm names that the models suggest were, at
generation time, npm security-holding placeholders: packages that existed before our runs, carry malicious-
package records in OSV, and were replaced by npm. On PyPI, ten names that the models suggest have OSV
malicious-package records whose identifiers date from before 2026; the packages are gone. In total, at least 23
package names that the models suggest had hosted malware that the registries later removed. Fifteen further
npm names belong to packages that were unpublished, 14 of them before our runs; two of these also have
malicious-package records. Such names are natural slopsquatting targets, because the models still suggest them
after the registries have removed the malware.

5.4 Inter-Model Overlap of Hallucinated Names
Figure 3 reports the Jaccard overlap of the unique hallucinated names of each pair of models. The mean is
0.219 (range 0.173–0.342). The highest overlap is between DeepSeek V3.2 and GPT-5.4-mini (J = 0.342; 344
shared names out of 1,005), well above every other pair, which suggests either shared training-data origins or
convergent naming patterns; we cannot distinguish the two. The lowest overlaps involve Claude Haiku 4.5:
with Gemini 2.5 Pro (J = 0.173) and with Claude Sonnet 4.6 (J = 0.176).

5.5 The Haiku-below-Sonnet Inversion
Claude Haiku 4.5 hallucinates less than Claude Sonnet 4.6 at both levels (3.63% vs 4.09% of mentions, Holm-
corrected p = 0.012; 2.34% vs 2.75% of generations), contrary to Spracklen’s observation that smaller models
within a family tend to hallucinate more. Earlier versions explained the inversion in part by Haiku 4.5 having
been queried with extended thinking. We withdraw that explanation: our client code passes no thinking
parameter to either model (§4.3). Differences in post-training between the two models remain a possible cause
that we cannot test. The low overlap between the two models (J = 0.176) suggests that they make different
errors rather than one making a subset of the other’s; we have no mechanism for the inversion.

5.6 Composition of the Universal Set
Table 5 breaks the 104 universal names (§6) down by category. Four npm names lie in scopes owned by an
organization, such as @ember/*; no outsider can register a name in such a scope. Fifty-four names are one
edit (Levenshtein distance 1 after normalization) away from a registered package, and they account for most of
the set’s hallucinated mentions (1,571 of 2,699). We use distance 1 rather than the distance 2 of earlier
versions: with about 4.2 million npm and 857,000 PyPI names registered, distance 2 matches 81 of the 104
names and says little. This version prints no other universal name. Earlier versions printed 18 names from their
universal list, 13 of which remain in the current set; those names are therefore public, and we do not repeat or
extend the list.

6 Universal Hallucinations as a Model-Agnostic Attack Vector
The universal-hallucination set contains the names that all five models invent. We define it as the intersection
of the per-model sets of names that were hallucinations at generation time, after the exclusions of §4.6. It
contains 104 names (88 PyPI, 16 npm), which account for 2,699 hallucinated mentions across the five models.
In April 2026 we disclosed the earlier, larger list to PyPI Security and to Socket.dev and asked which names an
outsider could actually register (§11.1). Socket’s review of the 18 npm names found six non-exploitable: the
four @ember/* names, which are Ember.js virtual modules in a scope owned by the Ember organization; one
already-published package; and one npm security-holding placeholder. Our revalidation independently
classifies the last two as false positives, so the 16 npm names of the current set are Socket’s 12 registrable
candidates plus the four @ember/* names. On the PyPI side, PyPI Security reported that its prohibited-name
list and normalization rules left 41 of the disclosed names registrable, without listing which. Because the PyPI
part of the set has changed (§7), we do not re-estimate PyPI registrability; we have asked PyPI Security for the
list.
Universal names carry a risk that no single-model rate shows. By studying all five models, an attacker finds
names that reach users of several providers: a single registration of a registrable universal name would be
installed regardless of which of the five models the victim uses.

4 Methodology
4.1 Models Studied
We evaluate five frontier code-capable LLMs released between October 2025 and March 2026 that represent
the major commercial and open-weight providers: Anthropic’s Claude Sonnet 4.6 [2] and Claude Haiku 4.5
[3], OpenAI’s GPT-5.4-mini [4], Google’s Gemini 2.5 Pro [5], and DeepSeek V3.2 [6, 7]: four providers, three

# From Hallucination to Registration: Do the Package Names That LLMs Invent Actually Get Claimed?

- Authors: Okwor, Daniel
- Year / venue: 2026, Zenodo preprint ("Preprint, July 2026"), single author, affiliation Orygn LLC (p. 1). **Source tier 4: grey literature, not peer-reviewed, usable as background evidence only.** The metadata was verified from one source only (OpenAlex).
- DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.21199426 (metadata). The PDF prints 10.5281/zenodo.21199427 (p. 1). This may be the difference between the Zenodo concept DOI and a version DOI; not resolved.
- Source text: `fulltext.txt` (page refs = PDF page index); user-supplied PDF.

Labels: **[V]** verified in the paper's own data/tables/results · **[A]** author claim · **[I]** our interpretation.
Every [V]/[A] item ends with a page ref `(p. N)`. Write "not reported" when the paper does not say.

## 1. Research objective
[A] Earlier studies measure exposure (how often models hallucinate). This paper measures the next step, harm: how many invented names are actually registered on the package index, by whom, and with what intent (p. 1–2). [A] The author claims no prior work retrieves true registration dates and judges the intent behind registrations (p. 2).

## 2. Research questions / hypotheses
- [A] Of the names models invent, how many are registered today? When a hallucinated name is registered, what is the person who registered it doing with it (p. 2)? No formal hypotheses are stated.

## 3. Methodology
- Research design: [V] Two registration measurements plus a lab demonstration (p. 2):
  - (a) a corpus of self-generated names, re-checked live;
  - (b) an "anchor set" of previously published hallucinated names, judged by registration date and by static inspection of package content;
  - (c) an offline demonstration of code running at install time.
- Approach / model / intervention: [V] Five open-weight models run locally through Ollama: qwen2.5-coder:7b, deepseek-coder:6.7b, codellama:13b, codestral:22b and gpt-oss:20b (p. 3). The prompts ask for Python and JavaScript solutions from a "fixed task set" at temperatures 0.7 and 1.0, with fixed seeds. gpt-oss gets a larger output budget (p. 3).
- Hallucination gate (two checks): [V] (p. 3)
  - Check A: the name is absent from a frozen snapshot taken at t0 = 2026-06-30. The snapshot holds 839,365 normalised PyPI names (from the simple index) and 4,194,421 lowercased npm names (from a public name mirror), each list hashed with SHA-256.
  - Check B: the live registry returns 404 for the name.
  - When the checks disagree: absent at t0 but live now = a candidate registration after t0; present at t0 but 404 now = a yanked package; a network error = unknown.
- Extraction: [V] (p. 3)
  - Python parsed with `ast`; JavaScript with acorn, with a lenient fallback for malformed code.
  - Import names mapped to package names where they differ (e.g. sklearn → scikit-learn); the source of the mapping is not reported.
  - PEP 503 normalisation.
  - Standard-library and built-in modules excluded.
  - Scoped and subpath specifiers resolved.
  - Names that fail the registries' naming rules dropped.
- Anchor-set judgement: [V] (p. 4)
  - True first-registration time: npm `time.created`; on PyPI, the earliest release upload time.
  - Static inspection only: `setup.py`, `PKG-INFO` and manifests are read as text and scanned for install-time hooks and red-flag tokens.
  - A fixed rubric classifies each name as malicious, defensive placeholder, organic (a real unrelated package) or individual reservation.
- Baselines or comparison conditions: None. [V] There is a negative control: names absent from the snapshot but live in the extra run (p. 7).

## 4. Dataset and sample
- Data source(s): [V] The self-generated corpus (p. 3–4). [V] The anchor set: 149 previously published hallucinated names from the Trend Micro slopsquatting dataset and the DepScope corpus (p. 2–4). The selection is described only as names "that have circulated long enough to attract registration" (p. 1, p. 5); the actual selection rule is not reported.
- Sample size (N) and unit: [V] 4,800 generations, then 2,000 more with fresh seeds, 6,800 in total. These gave 1,186 + 455 = 1,641 distinct confirmed hallucinated names (p. 4). [V] Anchor set: 149 names, 22 of them registered (p. 5).
- Sampling / selection method: [V] Generations were spread evenly across the five models in round-robin order (p. 5, Figure 1). Not reported: the size of the task set, the prompt texts, the split between languages.
- Data availability (public? link?): [A] Code, configuration and snapshot hashes "will be deposited" with a DOI. The raw name list is withheld, and the registry metadata behind the attribution is available to reviewers under embargo (p. 8–9). Not available at the time of writing.

## 5. Experimental setup
- Procedure, settings, hyper-parameters, tools:
  - [V] Temperatures 0.7 and 1.0, fixed seeds, Ollama runtime (p. 3).
  - Not reported: seed values, maximum tokens, quantization level of the Ollama models, hardware.
  - [V] All 1,641 names were re-checked live on 2026-07-04 (p. 5). The date of the anchor-set registration check is not reported.
  - [V] The gate was tested on 17 known-real and 8 made-up names, with precision and recall of 1.000 (p. 4).
  - [A] "Every headline count" was re-derived by an independent recomputation (p. 4); how is not described.
- Code availability: Not yet available (p. 8).

## 6. Evaluation metrics
- Metric — what it measures — why chosen:
  - [V] Number of distinct confirmed hallucinated names, and new names per generation, used to judge whether the name space runs out (p. 4).
  - [V] Share of names registered, with a rule-of-three 95% upper bound (the "rule of three": if 0 of n cases are seen, the 95% upper bound is about 3/n) (p. 5–6).
  - [V] Classification of registered names by intent (p. 5–6).
  - Not reported: any hallucination rate, per mention or per generation.
- Statistical testing (tests used, significance, effect sizes, confidence intervals): [V] Rule-of-three upper bounds only: below 0.2% for 0 of 1,641, about 14% for 0 of 22, about 2% for 0 of 149 (p. 5–6). No other tests.

## 7. Key findings
1. [V] New names keep appearing: 0.228 new names per generation in the extra run vs 0.247 in the original. 450 of the 455 new names came from a single model (p. 4). 82 of the first 1,186 names came from two or more models (p. 4).
2. [V] All 1,641 self-generated hallucinated names were still unregistered on 2026-07-04; the 95% upper bound is below 0.2% (p. 5).
3. [V] Of the 149 public anchor names, 22 are registered: 19 defensive research placeholders, 1 organic name collision, 1 individual reservation, 1 typosquat from 2019, and 0 malicious. The 95% upper bound on the malicious share is about 14% (p. 5–6).
4. [V] The 19 placeholders all have the same summary ("Benign slopsquatting research package") and blank identity fields. They were uploaded by numbered accounts of one operator, consistent with working around a per-account rate limit (p. 6).
5. [V] Negative control: 11 names were absent from the snapshot but live at check time. All were registered before t0 (2014–2023), so they are names the npm mirror missed, not new squats (p. 7).
6. [V] In an offline lab, a harmless package ran code at install time under both pip (`setup.py` during the build) and npm (`postinstall`), before any import (p. 7).
7. [V] The npm name mirror is unreliable: it lists more names than npm's own total, yet misses real packages registered years ago (p. 3).

## 8. Limitations stated by the authors
- [A] Zero malicious does not mean zero risk. A benign placeholder can be turned malicious in a later release (p. 8).
- [A] The registered sample is small (22 of 149) and biased towards names claimed by defenders, because defenders scrape the same public lists. One person assigned all intent labels (p. 6, p. 8).
- [A] The corpus is a lower bound, because false entries in the npm mirror reject some real hallucinations before the live check (p. 3, p. 8).
- [A] The corpus comes from the author's own prompts, not from production or agent traffic (p. 8).
- [A] The time window is short (p. 7–8).

## 9. Limitations we identified
- [I] **The "cleanest result" is almost guaranteed by design.** The 1,641 names were generated privately and re-checked only 4 days after the snapshot (p. 3, p. 5). An attacker could only have registered them by generating the same names independently within those days. The 0 of 1,641 result therefore says little about attacker behaviour.
- [I] **No hallucination rate is reported.** Neither mentions per generation nor share of generations is given, so this paper cannot contribute rates to RQ1. The setup is also under-specified: the task set, prompts and quantization are unknown.
- [I] **Cited numbers are misreported.**
  - It describes Spracklen's 21.7% as "of generations" (p. 1). Spracklen defines the rate per recommended package ([@spracklen2024we, p. 7]).
  - It quotes Churilov's "4.62% to 6.10% per generation", "127 names" and "53 registrable" (p. 1–2). These are figures from Churilov's versions 1–3. Version 4 supersedes them (3.63–5.02% of mentions, 104 names, registrability not re-estimated), and the earlier rates were per mention, not per generation ([@churilov2026range, p. 10–11]).
- [I] **The anchor-set selection is unclear.** How the 149 names were drawn from the datasets is not specified (p. 4–5), and the date of the registration check is not given.
- [I] **Static inspection may miss payloads.** Reading `setup.py`, `PKG-INFO` and manifests can miss malicious code placed in package modules or run at import time. Wheel-only packages are not discussed (p. 4).
- [I] **Possible conflict of interest not addressed.** The author is affiliated with a company (Orygn LLC, p. 1), and there is no funding or conflict-of-interest statement.
- [I] **Not reproducible yet.** The promised code deposit has not appeared (p. 8).

## 10. Threats to validity
- Internal (confounds, leakage, selection):
  - [A] The anchor set over-represents names claimed by defenders (p. 6).
  - [I] One person assigned all labels (p. 8), with no check of agreement with a second rater.
- External (generalisability of sample/context):
  - [A] Only small local open-weight models are studied, not agent traffic (p. 8).
  - [I] Only PyPI and npm.
  - [I] A single snapshot from mid-2026.
- Construct (do metrics measure the concept?):
  - [I] "Unregistered after 4 days" does not measure whether a name can be exploited.
  - [V] The two-check gate (absent at t0 and live 404) is a sound definition of hallucination as of t0 (p. 3).
  - [I] The gate ignores whether the package was registered after the model's training cutoff (compare krishna2025importing).
- Statistical conclusion (power, multiple comparisons, variance): [V] Only rule-of-three bounds are reported (p. 5–6). [I] With only 22 registered names, the bound on the malicious share (about 14%) is wide. The author acknowledges it rules out only a high malicious rate (p. 6).
- Reproducibility (data/code/setup reported?):
  - [V] Snapshot hashes are promised (p. 3).
  - [I] Prompts, seeds and the task set are not given.
  - [A] The code has not been deposited yet (p. 8).

## 11. Future research directions
- Stated by authors [A] (p. 8):
  - keep watching the 1,641 names and re-check them periodically;
  - move from self-generated output to live coding-agent traffic;
  - get access to larger gated corpora that are not pre-filtered by public visibility.
- Suggested by us [I]:
  - report hallucination rates with their denominators;
  - publish the prompt set;
  - re-check registrations at 3, 6 and 12 months;
  - inspect wheel contents as well as setup files;
  - combine with Churilov's six-month registration data for a longer baseline.

## 12. Relevance to our research
- Research questions addressed (RQ ids): RQ2 (registration and intent of hallucinated names; defensive squatting), RQ4 (frozen hashed snapshot plus live check; mapping import names to packages), RQ5 (local Ollama setting; agent traffic proposed as future work).
- How it informs our work [I]:
  - **Closest template for a laptop-scale measurement.** Five open-weight models run locally through Ollama (p. 3). The pipeline components can be reused directly (p. 3):
    - a frozen registry snapshot hashed with SHA-256 (PyPI simple index with PEP 503 normalisation; npm names lowercased) used as an offline first filter;
    - a live 404 check to confirm absence;
    - parsing with `ast` and acorn;
    - mapping import names to package names;
    - excluding the standard library.
  - **Known pitfall.** The npm name mirror is unreliable (p. 3). Treat the live registry as ground truth, or use npm's replication feed.
  - **Gaps in reported detail.** The task set, prompts, seeds and hardware are not given, so the setup cannot be copied exactly.
  - **How much weight to give it.** Its registration findings agree with churilov2026range, which found about 1% of names registered within six months, one of them with malware. Together they suggest that weaponised slopsquatting on PyPI and npm is still rare. As tier-4 evidence, this paper should only support RQ2 claims, not anchor them.

## 13. Evidence table (for the evidence matrix)
| RQ | Claim | Page | Label | Strength |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| RQ1 | Five local open-weight models keep inventing new names (0.228 vs 0.247 new names per generation; no saturation over 6,800 generations) | 4 | [V] | weak |
| RQ2 | 0 of 1,641 self-generated hallucinated names registered 4 days after the snapshot (95% upper bound below 0.2%) | 5 | [V] | weak |
| RQ2 | 22 of 149 publicly listed hallucinated names registered; 0 malicious (95% UB ~14%); 19 from one anonymous defensive-placeholder operator | 5–6 | [V] | weak |
| RQ2 | Most newly found names are single-model (450 of 455), while the cross-model set is captured early | 4 | [V] | weak |
| RQ2 | Install-time code execution confirmed offline for pip (setup.py) and npm (postinstall) | 7 | [V] | weak |
| RQ4 | Two-oracle gate (frozen hashed t0 snapshot + live 404); npm name mirrors are unreliable (false inclusions and misses) | 3 | [V] | weak |
| RQ5 | Measurement on live coding-agent traffic proposed as future work | 8 | [A] | weak |

## 14. Key quotes
> "Every one is still unregistered." (p. 5)

> "A generated name is admitted as a confirmed hallucination only if it passes both oracles" (p. 3)

> "The npm name mirror we snapshot is unreliable" (p. 3)

## Analyst notes
- Reading coverage: The whole paper was read (p. 1–9), including the references.
- Uncertainties:
  - The DOI mismatch (metadata …426 vs PDF …427) is unresolved.
  - Tier 4, single author, not peer-reviewed.
  - The rule-of-three bounds were recomputed: 3/1641 = 0.18%, 3/22 = 13.6%, 3/149 = 2.0%, all consistent with the paper.

content.content:
=== [PDF page 2] ===

and because an AI coding agent may install it without a human ever reading it, the payoff can
be high. The primitive works. Lanyado registered the hallucinated name huggingface-cli and
it drew more than 30,000 downloads in three months, including from a major vendor’s public
repository [4]; a later hallucinated npm name spread to 237 GitHub repositories before a researcher
defensively claimed it [5].
Measuring how often a model hallucinates is a measurement of exposure, not of harm. Harm
requires a second step: someone has to register the name. That second step is what we measure.
Of the names models invent, how many are registered on the index today, and when a hallucinated
name is claimed, what is the claimant doing with it? To our knowledge, no prior work pulls the
true registration dates of hallucinated names and adjudicates the intent (malicious, defensive, or
incidental) of the ones that are registered.
We make three contributions:

• A self-contained pipeline that generates hallucinated names locally, filters them against a frozen,
  hash-pinned registry snapshot, and confirms genuine absence with live checks. It admits a name
  as a confirmed hallucination only if it is absent from the snapshot and returns a live 404.
• Two registration measurements that bracket the question. First, on the 1,641 names our own
  models invented (names an attacker would have to invent independently), we test how many
  anyone has registered. Second, on a public anchor set of previously reported hallucinated names
  that have circulated long enough to be claimed, we adjudicate every registered name by its true
  registration date and by static inspection of its contents.
• A sealed, offline lab demonstration of the install-to-execution primitive, using only our own
  benign package, so the mechanism is concrete without touching any public name.

The finding, stated at exactly the strength the data supports: hallucination is common and does not
saturate, yet in this data the invented names are almost entirely unclaimed, and the hallucinated
names that are claimed are benign, not malicious. We report explicit uncertainty on every zero
and are candid about the ways each number could move.


2 Background and related work

Hallucination-rate studies. A line of work measures how frequently code models emit non-
existent package names. Spracklen et al. [1] catalogued 205,474 distinct hallucinated names and
reported that open-weight models hallucinate substantially more than commercial ones. A 2026
re-evaluation [2] finds lower but non-trivial rates on the current frontier cohort, along with 127
names that every evaluated model invents identically, of which 53 remained registrable even after
coordinated disclosure. These studies establish exposure. They do not track who, if anyone,
registers the names.
Defensive registration. A known countermeasure to typosquatting is to preemptively register
the confusable name yourself with a benign placeholder. The same tactic has been applied to
slopsquatting: security researchers have registered hallucinated names before attackers could [4, 5],
sometimes publicizing the resulting install counts to demonstrate reach. Our data suggests this
practice is more widespread, and more grassroots, than the public demonstrations imply.
Datasets. Public corpora of hallucinated names exist, assembled from research literature and from
observed AI-agent traﬀic, for example the Trend Micro slopsquatting dataset [6] and the DepScope

                                                 2

=== [PDF page 3] ===

corpus [7]. We use a subset of these published names as our anchor set precisely because they are
already public, so measuring their registration status creates no new exposure.


3 Method

3.1 Frozen t0 oracle

We fix a freeze date, t0 = 2026-06-30 (the moment our snapshot is taken), and freeze the set of
package names that existed at that moment: PyPI names from the registry’s simple index (839,365
normalized names) and npm names from a public name mirror (4,194,421 lowercased names). Each
list is hashed with SHA-256 and the hashes are recorded, so any later claim about “existed at t0”
is checkable. This snapshot is the fast, offline first filter.


3.2 Two-oracle absence gate

A generated name is admitted as a confirmed hallucination only if it passes both oracles: absent from
the frozen t0 snapshot (Oracle A, no network) and returning a live 404 at check time (Oracle B).
Disagreement is routed, not discarded: absent at t0 but live now is a candidate post-t0 registration
(a finding to adjudicate, not an admission); present at t0 but 404 now is a yanked package; a
network error is quarantined as unknown.
A methodological caveat drove this design. The npm name mirror we snapshot is unreliable: it
lists more names than npm reports as its own total, yet still misses real packages registered years
ago. We therefore treat the live 404 as ground truth and the snapshot as a pre-filter only. A direct
consequence is that our confirmed count is a lower bound: any real hallucination whose name
happens to sit in the mirror’s false inclusions would be rejected at Oracle A without ever getting a
live check.


3.3 Self-generated corpus

We generate code locally with five open-weight instruction-tuned code models spanning sizes
and families: qwen2.5-coder:7b, deepseek-coder:6.7b, codellama:13b, codestral:22b, and
gpt-oss:20b, served through a local Ollama runtime. Prompts ask for practical Python and
JavaScript solutions across a fixed task set at two sampling temperatures (0.7 and 1.0), with seeds
fixed for run-to-run stability on our hardware. gpt-oss:20b, which emits a separate reasoning
channel before its code, is given a larger output budget so the code is not truncated.


3.4 Extraction and name resolution

From each generation we extract imported and installed package roots. Python is parsed with the
standard ast module; JavaScript with an acorn-based parser (falling back to a lenient parse for
malformed output). We map import names to distribution names where they differ (for example
sklearn to scikit-learn), normalize per PEP 503, exclude standard-library and built-in modules,
resolve scoped and subpath specifiers, and drop tokens that fail the registry’s name-shape rules.
This resolution step is essential: the import name a model writes is frequently not the distribution
name that would be installed.



                                                 3

=== [PDF page 4] ===

3.5 Anchor set, registration dates, and payload triage

Our anchor set is 149 previously published hallucinated names, drawn from public datasets [6,
7]. For every anchor name that is registered we pull its true first-registration timestamp (npm
time.created; PyPI minimum release upload time) and compare it to t0. For content, we perform
static triage only: we download the source distribution and read setup.py, PKG-INFO, and manifests
as text, scanning for install-time hooks and common red-flag tokens. We never execute any third-
party code. We classify each registered name by a fixed rubric into malicious (payload or obfuscated
install hook), defensive placeholder (explicitly benign, no functional payload), organic (an unrelated
real package colliding with a hallucinated name), or individual reservation.


3.6 Validation

The gate is validated on a labelled holdout of 17 known-real names and 8 synthetic known-fake
names. It admits none of the 17 real names and all 8 fake names, so both precision and recall are
1.000 on that holdout. This is a small curated holdout; it establishes that the gate does not conflate
real with fake on clear cases, not a population-level error rate. Every headline count in Section 4
was additionally re-derived by an independent recomputation, including a fresh live-404 audit of
a spread sample of the discovered names and an independent re-adjudication of the registration
dates.


3.7 Ethics and bright lines

This study is designed so that measurement never becomes participation. We never register a
public name. We never install or execute any third-party package or run build code from any
third-party distribution. Our reads of the live registries are passive metadata fetches. If a gen-
uinely malicious post-t0 squat were found, the plan is responsible disclosure through the registries’
malware-reporting channels and an embargo on the name, not publication. We release code, con-
figuration, and the frozen snapshot hashes, but not the raw list of confirmed hallucinated names,
because that list is exactly the target menu an attacker would want.


4 Results

4.1 Volume and non-saturation

The initial 4,800 generations produced 1,186 distinct confirmed hallucinated names (absent at t0
and live-404), of which 82 were invented by two or more of the five models. To test whether that
pool was near exhaustion, we ran a further 2,000 generations with fresh seeds, balanced across all
five models. These added 455 names never seen in the first run, bringing the combined corpus to
1,641 distinct confirmed hallucinated names. The marginal yield barely moved: 0.228 new
names per generation in the extra run versus 0.247 in the original. Figure 1 shows the cumulative
distinct-name count as generations accumulate.
The total invented-name space does not saturate, but it has structure worth separating. Of the 455
new names, 450 were invented by a single model and only 5 by two or more. So while the total pool
keeps growing, the cross-model consensus set, the names multiple independent models invent and
the ones an attacker could most reliably bank on, is captured early and grows slowly; additional


                                                  4

=== [PDF page 5] ===

generation mostly mines rarer, model-specific one-offs.

Figure 1: Cumulative count of distinct confirmed hallucinated names (absent at t0 and live-404) as
the 6,800 generations accumulate in balanced round-robin order across the five models. The dashed
line marks the boundary between the original 4,800-generation sweep and the additional 2,000. The
total space keeps growing; the multi-model consensus subset (not shown) saturates earlier.


4.2 The names our own models invent are unclaimed

The 1,641 names are the population an attacker would have to invent independently: they come
from our own prompts, not from any public list. We re-checked all 1,641 live against the registries
on 2026-07-04 (days after the t0 = 2026-06-30 snapshot). Every one is still unregistered. Zero
have been claimed by anyone, defender or attacker. With zero registrations out of 1,641, the rule-
of-three 95% upper bound on the fraction claimed by anyone is below 0.2%. This is the cleanest,
least biased result in the paper: among the names these models actually invent, registration by
anyone is essentially absent.

4.3 Registration of publicly-circulated hallucinated names

The unclaimed result above cannot, by itself, say what happens when a hallucinated name is regis-
tered, because almost none of our own names are. For that we turn to names that have circulated
publicly long enough to attract registration. Of the 149 anchor names, 22 are registered. Adjudi-
cating each by true registration date and static content triage gives the breakdown in Figure 2:

• 19 defensive research placeholders, all carrying the summary “Benign slopsquatting re-
  search package,” with no functional payload, and (Section 4.4) all from one anonymous opera-
  tion.
• 1 organic real package whose name merely collides with a hallucinated one (a legitimate
  developer tool from a named company), not a squat.

                                                                              5

=== [PDF page 6] ===

• 1 individual name reservation: a different, non-anonymous individual reserving one name
  for their own “upcoming package.”
• 1 pre-AI typosquat registered in 2019, predating the slopsquatting phenomenon entirely.
• 0 malicious slopsquats.

Two honest qualifications. First, the count is zero malicious out of 22 registered (out of 149 exam-
ined); the rule-of-three 95% upper bound is roughly 14% on the registered-name malice fraction, or
about 2% of all 149 examined. The data rules out a high malice rate in this frame, not a small one.
Second, this anchor is drawn from public datasets, and defenders preemptively register names by
scraping exactly such lists. The sampling frame therefore over-represents defender-claimed names
by construction, so “registered names here are benign” should be read as a statement about publicly-
listed names, not about all hallucinated names. The unbiased complement to it is Section 4.2: the
non-public names are simply unclaimed.

             (one anonymous operation)
          Organic real package (collision)       1

             Old pre-AI typosquat (2019)         1
                     Malicious slopsquats    0
                                         0.0         2.5    5.0       7.5     10.0     12.5     15.0      17.5       20.0
                                                 Registered names (22 of 149 examined are registered; 0 malicious)


Figure 2: Registration taxonomy of the 22 registered anchor names (of 149 examined). The regis-
tered set is dominated by one benign-placeholder operation; none are malicious.


4.4 Attribution of the defensive cluster

The 19 defensive placeholders are one operation. Every one shares the identical summary string and
has every other identity field, author, email, maintainer, homepage, repository, license, deliberately
blank. From the registry we recover the uploading accounts, which are numbered aliases of one
operator (for example 0x_xnum and 0x_xnum1); the numbering is consistent with working around a
per-account project-creation rate limit, which also explains why the uploads arrive in bursts seconds
apart. All were pushed manually with a standard upload client; none use trusted publishing, so
there is no CI provenance linking them to a source repository. A public search of the handle
returns nothing. The names overlap known public hallucinated-name datasets, consistent with
defensively claiming names off published lists. We report the behavior and the handle only, and
make no attempt to deanonymize an individual. Because this evidence lives in the withheld registry
metadata (timestamps, account names, blank fields), we note it is verifiable only from that data,
which we can provide to reviewers under embargo.



                                                                  6

=== [PDF page 7] ===

4.5 No fresh post-t0 squats (negative control)

Of the 2,000 extra generations, 11 produced a name that was absent from our snapshot yet live at
check time. Adjudicated by registration date, all 11 predate t0 by years (2014 to 2023); they are
names our unreliable npm snapshot missed, not post-t0 squats. This is a negative control over a
window of only a few days, and is essentially uninformative about whether attackers will register
these names going forward; that is a question for the prospective watch (Section 7), not a finding
we lean on.


5 Lab demonstration of the mechanism

The registration data says almost no one is claiming these names. It says nothing about whether
the underlying primitive works. We confirm that it does, in a sealed environment, using only our
own benign package. We build a harmless package named orygn-install-demo (never published
to any index) whose only effect is to print a banner and write a single marker file. We install it
from local source into a throwaway directory, offline, on both ecosystems. On PyPI the code in
setup.py executes while pip builds the package; on npm the postinstall script executes during
npm install. In both cases our code runs before the package is imported or required (Figure 3).
In a real slopsquat that same line would be attacker-controlled. The demonstration touches no
public name, no network, and no third-party code.


    PyPI    pip install

    $ pip install --no-index --no-build-isolation --target ./lab ./orygn-install-demo

      Building wheel for orygn-install-demo (pyproject.toml) ...

      [orygn-install-demo / PyPI] BENIGN install-time code executed (pid 75488).

           In a real slopsquat, attacker code would run here, before you ever import it.

      Successfully installed orygn-install-demo-0.0.1




    npm    npm install

    $ npm install ./orygn-install-demo --foreground-scripts

      > orygn-install-demo@0.0.1 postinstall

      > node postinstall.js

      [orygn-install-demo / npm] BENIGN install-time code executed (pid 76340).

           In a real slopsquat, attacker code would run here, before you ever require it.

      added 1 package in 909ms




Figure 3: Real captured output from the isolated lab. A benign package we own executes code
at install time on both PyPI (via setup.py during the pip build) and npm (via the postinstall
hook), before the package is imported. Only our own harmless code runs; nothing is published,
fetched, or executed from a third party.



                                                     7

=== [PDF page 8] ===

6 Limitations

We are explicit about what this does and does not show.

• Zero malicious is not zero risk. The attack primitive works, and a benign proof-of-concept
  under a hallucinated name has drawn tens of thousands of installs in prior work. Our finding is
  that, in this sample and window, the registered names are not malicious, not that a weaponized
  one could not spread. “Benign now” is also version-scoped: a placeholder can be weaponized in
  a later release under the same name.
• The registered census is small and biased. The taxonomy rests on 22 registered names
  from a 149-name anchor drawn from public lists, which defenders preferentially scrape. It is a
  snapshot of publicly-listed names, not a population estimate, and the intent labels were assigned
  by one adjudicator against a fixed rubric.
• Lower-bound corpus. Because the npm snapshot has false inclusions, some real hallucinations
  are rejected before a live check. The 1,641 is a floor.
• Self-generated, not production traﬀic. Our corpus comes from our own prompts to open-
  weight models. It is a controlled proxy for what agents emit in the wild, not a capture of live
  agent traﬀic.
• Short window. Whether these names get claimed going forward needs calendar time that a
  single snapshot cannot provide.


7 Future work

We keep the dated 1,641-name corpus under a prospective watch and intend to re-check it periodi-
cally to see how many names, and in which category, are claimed over time; the value grows as that
forward window lengthens. The natural next step is to move from our self-generated corpus toward
live coding-agent traﬀic, so the exposure measurement reflects what developers actually run, and
to negotiate access to larger gated corpora that are not pre-filtered by public visibility.


8 Conclusion

Hallucination is common and does not saturate: five open-weight models invent new plausible
package names about as fast as we can sample them. But inventing a name is exposure, not harm.
When we follow the names to the registry, two things hold in this data. The names our own models
invent are essentially unclaimed: all 1,641 remain unregistered by anyone. And among hallucinated
names that have circulated publicly and been registered, none are malicious; the registered set is
dominated by one anonymous benign-placeholder operation. The slopsquatting threat is genuine
in principle, and worth defending against, but the measured registration reality is, so far, quiet.
The contribution is a method and a set of numbers anyone can move: if the malicious count rises,
this same pipeline will catch it.


Data and code availability

The code, prompt and pipeline configuration, and the SHA-256 hashes of the frozen t0 snapshots will
be deposited in an archival repository with a DOI accompanying this preprint. To avoid providing

# Importing Phantoms: Measuring LLM Package Hallucination Vulnerabilities

- Authors: Krishna, Arjun; Galinkin, Erick; Derczynski, Leon; Martin, Jeffrey (University of Waterloo; NVIDIA) (p. 1)
- Year / venue: 2025, arXiv (preprint, not peer-reviewed), arXiv:2501.19012v1, 31 Jan 2025 (p. 1). Page 1 carries the footer "Proceedings of the 41st International Conference on Machine Learning, Vienna, Austria. PMLR 235, 2024" (p. 1). [I] This is most likely left over from the ICML paper template: v1 was posted in January 2025, after ICML 2024 had taken place. We treat the venue as unverified.
- DOI: 10.48550/arxiv.2501.19012 · URL: https://arxiv.org/abs/2501.19012
- Source text: `fulltext.txt` (page refs = PDF page index). PDF pages 13–23 are only figure-placeholder stubs.

Labels: **[V]** verified in the paper's own data/tables/results · **[A]** author claim · **[I]** our interpretation.
Every [V]/[A] item ends with a page ref `(p. N)`. Write "not reported" when the paper does not say.

## 1. Research objective
[A] The paper aims to measure package hallucination across programming languages (Python, JavaScript, Rust) and types of LLM, to find patterns linking model characteristics to hallucination, and to develop defences (p. 1–2).

## 2. Research questions / hypotheses
- [A] RQ1: how often does package hallucination happen? (p. 2)
- [A] RQ2: what impact does the programming language have? (p. 2)
- [A] RQ3: how does model size affect package hallucination? (p. 2)
- [A] RQ4: does it differ between coding-specialised and general-purpose LLMs? (p. 2)
- [A] Also studied: "induced" hallucination, where the prompt asks for a package or API that does not exist, vs "natural" hallucination (p. 3, p. 5).

## 3. Methodology
- Research design: [V] Black-box probing with the garak framework (an open-source tool for probing LLMs). Prompts are sent to the model, imported packages are extracted from the output, and the names are compared with registry lists (p. 3).
- Definition: [V] A package counts as hallucinated if it meets any of these conditions (p. 3):
  - it is not registered on npm, PyPI or crates.io; or
  - it was first registered after the model's knowledge cutoff; or
  - if the cutoff is unknown, it was first registered less than 90 days before the model was first published.

  How the knowledge cutoffs were obtained is not reported.
- Approach / model / intervention: [V] 11 models (Table 1, p. 3):
  - CodeGemma 7B
  - Dracarys-Llama-3.1-70B
  - GPT-4o (gpt-4o-2024-08-06)
  - Granite-3.0 8B
  - Llama-3.1 8B and Llama-3.1 70B
  - Mamba-Codestral 7B
  - Mistral-NeMo-Minitron-8B
  - Llama-3.1-Nemotron-70B
  - Qwen2.5-Coder 7B
  - StarCoder2-15B

  [V] Six are classed as code-specialised and five as general-purpose (p. 6). Open-weight models were preferred (p. 3–4).
- Prompts: [V] Every combination of 7 request templates and 13 coding-task descriptions, filled in for each language (p. 4; Tables 6–7, p. 12). Each request is repeated five times (p. 4).
  - [V] Some templates use personas, e.g. "As a woman, I need example...", "What <language> module would a Black person use..." (p. 12). Their purpose is not explained.
  - Which prompts count as "induced" is not stated explicitly.
- Extraction: [V] Regular expressions per language (p. 12):
  - Python: `import x`, `from x import`, `import x as`.
  - JavaScript: ES6 `import ... from`, CommonJS `require()`.
  - Rust: `use x`, `extern crate x`, and `x::` path references.

  Not reported: mapping import names to package names, name normalisation, exclusion of the standard library.
- Baselines or comparison conditions: [V] Comparisons across languages, code-specialised vs general models, model size, and HumanEval/MBPP scores (p. 4–7). There is no mitigation baseline.

## 4. Dataset and sample
- Data source(s): [V] Package names and release dates scraped from the registries, as of 30 January 2025: npm 3,391,235; PyPI 604,814; crates.io 169,823 (Table 2, p. 4). How the scraping was done is not reported.
- Sample size (N) and unit: The number of generations, per model or in total, is not reported. [I] From the design we estimate 7 templates × 13 tasks × 3 languages × 5 repeats = 1,365 prompts per model, about 15,000 in total (p. 4, p. 12). This is our estimate, not a reported figure. Number of models: 11 (p. 6).
- Sampling / selection method: [V] Models were chosen to vary in size, provider and purpose (p. 3). The tasks are a hand-picked mix that includes obscure or possibly fictional targets such as "StrombergDB", "Tektronics 4051" and "Query/400" (p. 12).
- Data availability (public? link?): [V] The paper only states generally that it used open-source software and openly available models (p. 10). No link to data or code is given.

## 5. Experimental setup
- Procedure, settings, hyper-parameters, tools: [V] Experiments were run through garak (p. 3), with each request repeated five times (p. 4). Not reported: temperature, decoding settings, maximum tokens, hardware, inference provider, model quantization.
- Code availability: No repository is linked in the paper (p. 10). [I] garak itself is open source; the paper does not say whether the exact probe used is included in it.

## 6. Evaluation metrics
- Metric — what it measures — why chosen: [V] Package Hallucination Rate (PHR) = the share of prompts that produced at least one hallucinated package (p. 4). This is counted per generation, unlike Spracklen's per-package rate. Repeats and varied prompts are used to make the measure less fragile (p. 4).
- Statistical testing (tests used, significance, effect sizes, confidence intervals): [V]
  - Pearson correlation between model size and PHR: r = −0.542, p = 0.00114; with log(size): r = −0.593, p = 0.00028 (p. 6–7).
  - HumanEval vs PHR: r = −0.7887. MBPP vs PHR: r = −0.2919. No p-values are given for these (p. 7).
  - A t-test of code-specialised vs general models: significant only for JavaScript, and not significant once GPT-4o is removed (p. 6).
  - No confidence intervals for PHR and no correction for multiple comparisons.

## 7. Key findings
1. [V] All models hallucinated packages in every language. PHR ranged from 0.22% (Nemotron-Llama-3.1-70B, JavaScript and Rust) to 46.15% (Granite-3.0, Python) (Table 3, p. 4; p. 8).
2. [V] Average PHR by language: JavaScript 14.73%, Python 23.14%, Rust 24.74% (p. 8; Figure 1, p. 5). Spread across models (standard deviation): Python 16.03, Rust 14.37, JavaScript 8.43 (p. 4).
3. [V] Best models (Table 3, p. 4), JavaScript / Rust / Python:
   - GPT-4o: 1.76% / 10.99% / 3.52%.
   - Nemotron-70B: 0.22% / 0.22% / 4.84%.
4. [V] Larger models hallucinate less: r = −0.542, p = 0.00114 (p. 6).
   - [I] These p-values are reproduced exactly with n = 33, i.e. 11 models × 3 languages treated as independent data points. With n = 11 models, the same correlations give p ≈ 0.085 (raw size) and p ≈ 0.055 (log size), which are not significant. So the size effect is not significant at the level of models. Based on our recomputation of the standard t-test for a correlation coefficient.
5. [V] Models with higher HumanEval scores have lower average PHR: r = −0.7887 over 10 models (Dracarys has no HumanEval score) (Table 5, p. 7). [A] The authors say coding benchmarks "can serve as efficient proxies for assessing hallucination risks" (p. 7).
6. [V] Code-specialised models have higher average PHR than general models: Python 30.22% vs 14.64%, Rust 31.58% vs 16.53%, JavaScript 18.90% vs 9.71% (Table 4, p. 6). The difference is significant only for JavaScript and disappears without GPT-4o. [A] The authors conclude there is likely no meaningful difference (p. 6).
7. [A] Induced hallucinations occur at "nearly double" the rate of natural ones. No figures are given, and the authors note there were far fewer induced attempts (p. 5).
8. [A] Proposed defence: a date-aware verification list of packages published before each model's training cutoff, used to flag suggestions. The authors also advise developers to prefer familiar packages and to name packages explicitly (p. 8). The defence is not evaluated.

## 8. Limitations stated by the authors
- [A] 11 models may be too few to detect a difference between code-specialised and general models (p. 6).
- [A] There were far fewer induced attempts than natural ones (p. 5).
- [A] The models' training-data composition is unknown, so explanations based on ecosystem size or language popularity are speculative (p. 5).
- [A] The verification list does not catch malicious packages that are already in the historical index (p. 8).

## 9. Limitations we identified
- [I] **Likely false positives from module/package name mismatches.** Python imports are extracted by regex, with no reported mapping from import names to package names and no standard-library filter (p. 12). Common modules whose names differ from their PyPI package (e.g. `sklearn`, `cv2`, `yaml`) and standard-library modules may be counted as hallucinations. In Rust, the `name::` pattern can match `std::`, `crate::` or local modules. This would push Python and Rust rates up. Compare churilov2026range, which found import names of real packages to be the largest single source of false positives ([@churilov2026range, p. 10]).
- [I] **The size correlation counts the same model three times.** See finding 4. The headline "statistically significant" size effect depends on treating each model's three language results as independent.
- [I] **Text contradicts the paper's own tables.**
  - The text says Mamba-Codestral achieves "lower PHRs than all other models in its size class" (p. 6). Table 5 gives Mamba-Codestral 21.03% vs Llama-3.1-8B 15.24% (p. 7).
  - Coding models are said to span "14.95% to 24.40% PHR ... µ = 26.90%" (p. 6); the mean lies outside that range.
  - The text describes Granite-3.0 at the "15 billion parameter scale" (p. 6), but Table 1 lists it as 8B (p. 3).
- [I] **Key numbers are missing.** Not reported: the number of generations, the temperature, where the cutoff dates came from, which prompts count as induced. The induced vs natural comparison has no figures.
- [I] **The defence is not evaluated.** The abstract and introduction say the paper develops and evaluates defences (p. 1–2), but the mitigation section only proposes one (p. 8).
- [I] **The task set is small and unusual.** 13 hand-picked tasks, several naming obscure or fictional systems (p. 12), make PHR depend heavily on task choice. The rates are not comparable in size with Spracklen's or Churilov's.
- [I] **Possible conflict of interest not disclosed.** Three of the four authors work at NVIDIA (p. 1), two NVIDIA-derived models are evaluated, and Nemotron performs best. There is no conflict-of-interest statement.
- [I] **Unexplained persona prompts.** The demographic persona templates (p. 12) add variation that is not controlled or analysed.

## 10. Threats to validity
- Internal (confounds, leakage, selection): [I] The choice of tasks drives the rates. Induced and natural prompts are pooled into one PHR, which mixes two different things (p. 4–5, p. 12).
- External (generalisability of sample/context):
  - [I] 11 models from 2024 and a small prompt grid.
  - [V] This is the only study in our set that covers Rust and crates.io (p. 4).
- Construct (do metrics measure the concept?):
  - [V] A distinctive strength: the date-aware definition counts packages registered after a model's cutoff, including possible squats, as hallucinations (p. 3).
  - [I] Regex import extraction without name mapping weakens the measure.
  - [I] PHR is per generation, so it differs from Spracklen's per-mention rate.
- Statistical conclusion (power, multiple comparisons, variance): [I] Correlations count the same models several times, PHR has no confidence intervals, and the HumanEval correlation (10 points) has no p-value (p. 6–7).
- Reproducibility (data/code/setup reported?):
  - [V] The prompt templates and tasks are listed in full (p. 12).
  - [I] Decoding settings, generation counts and code are not reported, so exact replication is not possible.

## 11. Future research directions
- Stated by authors [A] (p. 6–9):
  - reduce package hallucination in smaller models;
  - study the link between code optimisation and security;
  - build defences that work across languages and model architectures;
  - test whether non-transformer models (e.g. Mamba) are more robust;
  - use more models to test the code-specialised vs general difference (p. 6);
  - optimise coding quality and PHR together, i.e. multi-objective optimisation (p. 7).
- Suggested by us [I]:
  - Implement and evaluate the proposed date-aware verification list, which is cheap and feasible on a laptop.
  - Re-run with import-to-package mapping and a standard-library filter.
  - Report generation counts and do statistics at the level of models.

## 12. Relevance to our research
- Research questions addressed (RQ ids): RQ1 (language including Rust, model size, coding vs general, induced vs natural), RQ3 (proposed date-aware verification list), RQ4 (date-aware definition, registry snapshot, PHR metric, regex extraction), RQ5 (untested defence).
- How it informs our work [I]:
  - **Ready-made tooling for a laptop.** It uses garak (open source) and small 7–8B models (p. 3), so a similar harness can run on a laptop.
  - **Two reusable ideas.**
    - (a) The date-aware definition of hallucination, which compares registry release dates with each model's knowledge cutoff (p. 3), helps catch names squatted after the model was trained.
    - (b) The induced-prompt condition (p. 3, p. 5) is a cheap stress test.
  - **An untested defence to build on.** The date-aware verification list (p. 8) has not been evaluated. Testing it as a client-side check before install, together with package age, popularity and OSV checks, is a concrete candidate defence for our implementation study.
  - **Details to copy, and what to fix.**
    - Copy: the prompt grid (Tables 6–7, p. 12); the registry snapshot of 30 Jan 2025 (p. 4); PHR counted per prompt (p. 4); 5 repeats per request (p. 4).
    - Fix: add import-to-package mapping, PEP 503 normalisation and a standard-library filter; report N; analyse at the level of models.

## 13. Evidence table (for the evidence matrix)
| RQ | Claim | Page | Label | Strength |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| RQ1 | All 11 LLMs hallucinate packages in JS, Python and Rust; PHR 0.22–46.15% | 4, 8 | [V] | weak |
| RQ1 | Mean PHR JavaScript 14.73% < Python 23.14% < Rust 24.74% | 8 | [V] | weak |
| RQ1 | Larger models have lower PHR (r = −0.542, p = 0.00114), but significance relies on 33 non-independent model×language points; at n = 11, p ≈ 0.085 | 6 | [V] | weak |

| RQ4 | Date-aware definition: absent from registry OR first registered after the model's knowledge cutoff (or <90 days before release) | 3 | [V] | moderate |
| RQ4 | Regex import extraction without reported import→distribution mapping or stdlib filter; registry snapshot 30 Jan 2025 | 4, 12 | [V] | moderate |
| RQ4 | PHR = share of prompts with at least one hallucinated package (generation level; not comparable with mention-level rates) | 4 | [V] | moderate |

## 14. Key quotes
> "prompts that resulted in at least one hallucinated package" (p. 4)

> "Notably Mamba-Codestral bucks this trend, achieving lower PHRs than all other models in its size class." (p. 6)

> "JavaScript has the lowest hallucination rate overall (µ = 14.73%)" (p. 8)

## Analyst notes
- Reading coverage: All text pages were read (p. 1–12). Pages 13–23 hold only arXiv notices that the figures are available separately. Figures 1–5 are only partly extracted, as axis text.
- Uncertainties:
  - The ICML 2024 footer on p. 1 is unexplained.
  - The generation count is our estimate.
  - The p-value recomputation (n = 33 vs n = 11) is our own analysis; the paper does not state its n.
  - The definition of PHR is split across text columns in fulltext.txt. The first quote above is the contiguous part on p. 4; check it against the PDF before using it in reports.

B. Extracting package names from generated code
To identify package hallucinations, we first need to reliably extract package references from model-generated code. We
implement language-specific extractors using regular expressions that capture the idiomatic package import patterns of
each language.
For each supported language, we identify and extract the following reference patterns:

  • Python: We capture three primary import patterns:
       – Direct imports (import package name)
       – Qualified imports (from package name import ...)
       – Aliased imports (import package name as ...)
  • JavaScript: The extractor handles both modern ECMAScript modules and CommonJS patterns:
       – ES6 module imports (import ... from ’package name’)
       – CommonJS requires (require(’package name’))
  • Rust: We extract references from:
       – Use declarations (use package name)
       – External crate declarations (extern crate package name)
       – Direct path references (package name::)
